title.zh: Brill Building的流行音乐创作模式

summary.en: The Brill Building model returns music to an era when songwriters and performers are separate roles.
summary.zh: Brill Building模式让音乐重回了由歌曲创作者和表演者分离的时代。

body.zh:
Brill Building模式让音乐重回了由歌曲创作者和表演者分离的时代。

这节课，我们从Brill Building的流行音乐模式讲起。在很多方面，Brill Building都是第一章提到的传统流行音乐模式（Tin Pan Alley模式）的继承者。该模式侧重音乐发行，是由音乐创作者及利益所推动的音乐模式。事实上，大部分Tin Pan Alley歌曲创作者在Brill Building都有自己的工作室。我们总说起Brill Building，但事实上很多人的工作室却不在这里。Brill Building位于百老汇大街1619号，但你得走到第51街，到百老汇1650号，才能看到那些人的工作室。

Brill Building模式带我们重回了由歌曲创作者负责创作、表演者负责表演、发行者负责发行的时代。这个阶段兴起了唱片制作人（producer）这个新角色。Jerry Leiber和Mike Stoller大概是60年代The Beatles和Bob Dylan到来之前，摇滚历史最重要的歌曲创作者。Leiber和Stoller在洛杉矶开始创作的，他们是两个真正融入洛杉矶非裔美国人社区的白人，交黑人女友，去黑人常去的俱乐部，也一直受到尊重。如Jerry Leiber所说，“我们认为自己就是黑人了，虽然实际上不是这样，但我们当时就是这么想的。”因此，他们把很多的R&B实践投入到了歌曲创作中，曾有段时间为Spark Records写歌，并且为洛杉矶的很多乐队写歌并录制。他们跟The Robins和Big Mama Thornton合作过。《You Ain't Nothin’ but a Hound Dog》这首歌是他们为Big Mama Thornton写的，后来这被Elvis翻唱。Big Mama Thornton演唱这首歌是在1953年，有意思的是，Elvis翻唱的并不是Leiber和Stoller当初为Big Mama Thornton写的版本，而是Elvis在拉斯维加斯旅行时听到的一位歌手的版本，那个版本改动了原版的歌词，Jerry Leiber说他从未写过“you ain't never caught a rabbit and you ain't no friend of mine”这句歌词。

突然间，Leiber和Stoller拥有了一首大热歌曲，成为了音乐产业中的大腕，获得了一些权力和能力，可以更加随心所欲。他们开始和一个叫做The Coasters的组合合作，其实就是新版的The Robins，只不过从西海岸搬到了东海岸而已。不是所有The Robins的成员都想离开洛杉矶，有几个跟着Leiber和Stoller来到了纽约，开始与Atlantic Records合作。他们签署了一份独立协议，在与Atlantic Records合作的同时，也可以与其他公司合作。他们不仅创作歌曲，也可以开始创作唱片。他们在写歌的同时，考虑了这张唱片的录制方式以及乐器之间如何配合。这在当时看来是不寻常的。通常来说，歌曲创作者负责写歌，但歌曲最后录制出来的效果，却是由其他人比如编曲人或音乐人所决定的，但是他们在创作的时候就构思这首歌的录制方式了。他们对The Coasters这个组合最有雄心壮志，合作期间，他们借用了百老汇的曲目和理念。The Coasters可以把这些叙事歌曲表演出来，他们称之为短剧(playlet)。Jerry Leiber和Mike Stoller就只需要做好歌曲创作者，不用太担心制作人的问题，我们之后还会说到这个。他们是活跃于20世纪50到60年代最重要的两位歌曲创作者之一，住在纽约，出没于Brill Building附近。

我们接下来要谈到歌曲创作者，都集结在百老汇大街1650号一家叫做Aldon Publishing的公司里。我前面提到过，在Brill Building附近街区，有好几个相关的工作室，Aldon Publishing就是其中之一。它是由Al Nevins和Don Kirschner共同建立的，他们运作公司的方式十分老派。歌曲创作者呆在一个个有钢琴的小隔间里，你可以透过墙听到里面的音乐，到一天结束的时候，他们就把自己写的歌拿出来，然后大家进行竞争，争抢录制唱片的机会，公司会决定要向哪个创作团队购买作品。所以Aldon Publishing公司就像是流行音乐创作的大卖场。

有些重要的歌曲创作者出自那里，比如Gerry Goffin和Carole King。我们之后还会再提到Carole King，她后来成为了70年代最重要的歌曲创作者之一，她的职业光辉之路绵延了好几十年。Gerry Goffin和Carole King写的第一首大热单曲是The Shirelles唱的《Will You Love Me Tomorrow》，曾在1960年登上榜首。1961年他们又为Little Eva写了登顶的《The Locomotion》。我记得这个歌手最开始是Gerry Goffin和Carole King的保姆，之后他们发现她的音乐天赋，于是让她唱了《The Locomotion》。还有一首有意思的歌是The Cookies在1962年演唱的《Chains》，后来被The Beatles翻唱。我们通常并不觉得The Beatles与女子组合（girl groups）有什么关系，但实际上，他们从女子组合身上吸取了很多。

Jeff Barry和Ellie Greenwich是Aldon公司麾下另一个歌曲创作团队，两首大热歌曲是1963年Ronettes演唱的《Be My Baby》，及同年Crystals演唱的《Da Doo Ron Ron》；Cynthia Weil和Barry Mann在1962年为Crystals写了热单《Uptown》；另外Neil Sedaka和Howie Greenfield 1961年的《Calendar Girl》也是也红极一时，他们的《Breaking Up Is Hard To Do》在1962年登顶榜首。 Neil Sedaka和Howie Greenfield的很多歌曲，都是由Neil Sedaka自己演唱的，他算是当时的青少年偶像。有趣的是《Breaking Up Is Hard To Do》这首歌在1975年再度回归，Neil Sedaka对它做了全新改编，这也让他在70年代打开了事业的新局面。

前面提到的这些歌曲创作者一首接一首地写流行歌，一首接一首的制作，为Aldon公司服务的。由此，你对Brill Building的商业模式应该就有所体会了。从现在开始，只要再提到Brill Building，指的就是这种专门为青少年市场创作歌曲的专业环境，歌曲创作者和演唱者分离的模式（虽然有Neil Sedaka和Carol King这种个例，但是大多数的歌曲创作者都不是演唱者）。
body.en:
The Brill Building model returns music to an era when songwriters and performers are separate roles.

This lecture starts with Brill Building pop. In many ways it inherits the Tin Pan Alley model from Chapter 1: publishing-led, driven by writers and their commercial interests. In fact most Tin Pan Alley writers keep rooms in or around Brill Building. We say “Brill Building,” but many studios are not in that tower. Brill Building is 1619 Broadway; you often walk to 51st Street, 1650 Broadway, to find the rooms that matter.

The model restores writer / performer / publisher division of labor. A new role also rises: the producer. Jerry Leiber and Mike Stoller are among the most important rock songwriters before the Beatles and Bob Dylan in the 1960s. They start in Los Angeles as white writers who really enter Black communities—Black girlfriends, Black clubs, and lasting respect. As Leiber put it, they thought of themselves as Black even though they were not. They pour R&B practice into writing, work for Spark Records, and write and record for many L.A. acts—the Robins, Big Mama Thornton. “Hound Dog” is theirs for Thornton; Elvis later covers it. Thornton cuts it in 1953; interestingly Elvis does not cover their Thornton version but a Las Vegas singer’s rewrite. Leiber says he never wrote the line “you ain’t never caught a rabbit and you ain’t no friend of mine.”

Suddenly Leiber and Stoller have a smash, industry clout, and freer hands. They work with the Coasters—essentially a new Robins moved east. Not all Robins want to leave L.A.; some follow them to New York and Atlantic. They sign an independent deal that lets them work with Atlantic and others. They write songs and also shape records—how a track will be cut and how instruments lock. That is unusual: writers usually stop at the song; arrangement and sound belong to others. With the Coasters they borrow Broadway ideas; narrative songs become “playlets.” As writers they can focus on songs without fretting as much about production—we return to that later. They are among the key 1950s–60s writers, living in New York near Brill Building.

Other writers cluster at Aldon Publishing, 1650 Broadway—one of several houses in the neighborhood, founded by Al Nevins and Don Kirshner in an old-school way. Writers sit in tiny piano cubicles; you hear music through the walls; at day’s end songs compete for recording slots and the company buys from winning teams. Aldon is a pop-songwriting bazaar.

Major teams come out of it. Gerry Goffin and Carole King—King later becomes one of the 1970s’ most important writers, with a multi-decade arc. Their first big hit is the Shirelles’ “Will You Love Me Tomorrow” (No. 1, 1960); in 1961 they top the chart with Little Eva’s “The Loco-Motion”—Eva had been their babysitter before they heard her talent. The Cookies’ 1962 “Chains” is later covered by the Beatles; we seldom link the Beatles to girl groups, but they learned a lot from them.

Jeff Barry and Ellie Greenwich write the Ronettes’ 1963 “Be My Baby” and the Crystals’ “Da Doo Ron Ron”; Cynthia Weil and Barry Mann write the Crystals’ 1962 “Uptown”; Neil Sedaka and Howie Greenfield score with 1961’s “Calendar Girl” and top 1962 with “Breaking Up Is Hard to Do.” Sedaka often sings their songs himself—a teen idol. In 1975 he remakes “Breaking Up Is Hard to Do” and reopens a 1970s career.

These writers grind hit after hit for Aldon. That is the Brill Building business: from now on the name means a professional teen-market song factory with writer/performer split (Sedaka and Carole King are exceptions; most writers are not the singers).
